claim: The reporter behind a Mona Lisa forgery tale once sawed through prison bars.

knots.passage: French poet Guillaume Apollinaire came under suspicion and was arrested and imprisoned. Apollinaire implicated his friend Pablo Picasso, who was brought in for questioning. Both were later exonerated. The real culprit was Louvre employee Vincenzo Peruggia, who had helped construct the painting's glass case. He carried out the theft by locking himself in the Louvre building and removing the painting, remaining unnoticed due to the Louvre being closed for that day.
knots.hatnote: In 1911 the Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre, and Paris suspected poets.

knots.passage: A year after the theft, Saturday Evening Post journalist Karl Decker wrote that he met an alleged accomplice named Eduardo de Valfierno, who claimed to have masterminded the theft. Forger Yves Chaudron was to have created six copies of the painting to sell in the US while concealing the location of the original. Decker published this account of the theft in 1932.
knots.hatnote: The plain story wasn't enough for one American magazine writer.

knots.passage: Karl Decker, pen name Charles Duval, (died 1941, age 73) was a journalist in the United States who worked for William Randolph Hearst's New York Journal. He covered events leading up to the Spanish American War and helped Evangelina Cosio y Cisneros escape from a Spanish prison.
knots.hatnote: Decker had pulled off a far bolder caper of his own, years earlier.

knots.passage: Cosio suggested drugging her jail-mates so they would sleep through the night and breaking out one of the bars to make her escape. Decker had a room rented in the building next door and at night had a ladder stretched from the roof of that building to the roof of the jail. He and his associates, over two nights, climbed over to the roof of the jail and sawed through one of the bars, which created a large enough opening for the slight prisoner to squeeze through and escape.
knots.hatnote: In Havana, a young prisoner and a newspaperman plotted together.

knots.passage: The young woman was taken to the home of one of the conspirators, Carlos Carbonell, an American educated, Cuban banker. After three days of hiding from the police-conducted searches, Cosio, dressed as a man, with her abundant hair stuffed under a large hat, and carrying an unlit cigar, walked through Havana to the dock, boarded a New York bound ship using false identification papers, and escaped to the United States.
knots.hatnote: Getting out of jail was only half of it.

payoff: The man who sold America a doubtful tale of six fake Mona Lisas had once staged a very real escape himself.
caveats: Wikipedia's Eduardo de Valfierno article says Decker's story is the only source for Valfierno and Chaudron and casts serious doubt on it.
